newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: INTERVIEW-Bangladesh sugar industry faces crisis.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Bangladesh sugar industry faces crisis.

text.p: 1996/97 sugar production was expected to fall by 25 percent because of a shortage of cane exacerbated by farmers turning to other crops or molasses, the state-owned Bangladesh Sugar and Food Industries Corp says.

Corporation chairman A.K. Munshi told Reuters on Wednesday that losses in 15 sugar mills, all in the public sector, might double to 700 million taka ($16 million) in the 1996/97 fiscal year, against the previous year. The fiscal year ends on June 30.

"This is mainly due to production shortfall. There is also (the problem of) excess manpower. We have stopped recruitment and 885 employees have been sent on early retirement," Munshi said. Floods, misuse of fertiliser and pesticides and "grower apathy" hit sugar production this year, he said. Munshi also said farmers were opting for the more lucrative molasses market rather than selling their cane to mills.
"This is because they get cash immediately and the price is attractive," he said.

"Molasses is also smuggled into India and Burma, and believed to be used for making wine," he said. Munhsi said many farmers were now growing wheat for a higher return than sugar. He said the target for sugar production was set at 215,000 tonnes for 1996/97 against an actual yield of 180,000 tonnes in 1995/96. The country is expected to set the sugar production target for 1997/98 at 215,000 tonnes. Bangladesh plans to import 57,000 tonnes of white
sugar by October. The country has already imported 93,000 tonnes of sugar out of an import target of 150,000 tonnes for fiscal 1996/97.
A bidding for 25,000 tonnes of sugar was due on Sunday. Munshi said Bangladesh's annual sugar requirement was 360,000 tonnes.

He said the government was planning to sell three sugar mills. Tenders for two had already been floated. The government's policy to sell 49 percent shares in the 15 other state-owned sugar mills through the stock exchange opened up an opportunity for the private sector, Munshi said. "The private sector should come up to set up sugar mills. There is a secured domestic market. This may be attractive to the private entrepreneurs," Munshi said.
